\section{Q1: What explains a plot's persistent departure from the shared curve?}

Using the 4-survey cohort, canopy cover and thinning history dominate the attribution in every feature set and every method tested (Table~\ref{tab:results-q1}).

% AUDIT: Q1's modelled population is not restricted to mature stands (age >= 30 in 2023), unlike Q2 and Q3, which both apply this filter (Table~\ref{tab:data-cleaning-funnel}, row 7 -- 71,766 plots pre-filter vs. 58,112 post-filter, 4-survey). A direct check (Set4, EN/XGBoost, 5-fold spatial CV) found this increases R2 by roughly 0.05 (EN: 0.358 to 0.406) to 0.07 (XGBoost: 0.395 to 0.460) -- the headline numbers reported here are therefore conservative relative to a maturity-filtered population, not overstated. Full re-derivation across all sets and downstream checks (VIF, ICC, SHAP, ablations) was not undertaken given time constraints.

These $R^2$ values are modest in absolute terms: even the best set (Set2, XGBoost, $R^2=0.416$) leaves more than half the variation in a plot's persistent curve departure unexplained by the tested environmental and management features. The value of these models lies in identifying which conditions are associated with departures, not in precisely predicting how large a given plot's departure will be. $R^2$ is not directly comparable between Q1 and Q2, or between Q1/Q2 and Q3: each predicts a different target with different underlying variance, so a higher or lower number in one section does not by itself mean a stronger or weaker model.

Before the attribution question itself, Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig4-trajectories} grounds what "persistent departure from the shared curve" actually looks like in observed data, for six example plots spanning the residual distribution.

\subsection{Discussion}
\textbf{Canopy cover and thinning history dominate the attribution in every feature set and both methods -- but because canopy cover comes from the same LiDAR pipeline as the height targets, this could just be the target restated in different units.} Canopy cover carries the largest or near-largest Elastic Net coefficient in every set (Set4: +1.943$\pm$0.034), and ranks first by mean $|$SHAP$|$ in every XGBoost set (1.375--1.442).

This raises an obvious concern: canopy cover is measured from the same LiDAR survey as the height target itself, so a large coefficient could just mean the model has found a disguised copy of the target, not a real driver. Three checks test this directly, shown together in Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig1-canopycover-ablation}. First, canopy cover's correlation with all three of this project's targets is moderate (Pearson 0.35--0.47), not near 1 -- it is not simply the target restated in different units. Second, removing canopy cover from Set4 and refitting drops $R^2$ by roughly a third for both models (Elastic Net: 0.350 to 0.231; XGBoost: 0.388 to 0.249; Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig1-canopycover-ablation}, left) -- a bigger drop than its SHAP margin alone (1.2--1.7$\times$ the next variable) would suggest, meaning it carries signal nothing else in the set backfills. Third, the variable most likely to absorb that gap, $\mathit{dist}_{\text{to\_road}}$, does not: its own SHAP value moves slightly the wrong way (1.003 to 0.869; Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig1-canopycover-ablation}, right). Together, these rule out simple correlation-driven credit transfer as the mechanism, though they do not explain why canopy cover carries this much unique signal in the first place.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_results/q1/q1_final_fig1_canopycover_ablation.png}
\caption{\textbf{CanopyCover carries real, non-redundant signal.} Left: pooled $R^2$ (Set4, 4-survey) with vs.\ without CanopyCover for Elastic Net and XGBoost -- both lose roughly a third of their explanatory power. Right: mean $|$SHAP$|$ for CanopyCover, $\mathit{dist\_to\_road}$, precipitation and slope, with vs.\ without CanopyCover -- $\mathit{dist\_to\_road}$'s importance does not rise to compensate, evidence against simple correlation-driven credit transfer. The ``without'' condition is a genuine live re-run, not a transcription of an earlier result.}
\label{fig:q1-fig1-canopycover-ablation}
\end{figure}

The defensible reading: treat canopy cover and thinning as baseline stand-structure controls, expected to dominate by construction. The actual attribution question is what the true environmental variables contribute beyond that baseline.

\textbf{Most Set~4 predictors agree across models, while six reveal sharp divergences anchored by TOPEX (Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig2-attribution-lenses}).} % AUDIT: corrected 2026-08-21 -- this headline previously said "only slope is stable," which undersold how many variables agree and undercounted how many disagree. A full 19-variable check (Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}) found 6 with real EN/LMM disagreement, not just topex/tas_mean/soilgrids_ph as originally discussed; the rest, including slope_degrees, show sign agreement.
Across the abiotic predictors evaluated in detail, $\mathit{slope\_degrees}$ and $\mathit{chelsa\_bio12\_precip\_mm}$ remain stable across methods, displaying consistent positive signs and comparable magnitudes in both LMM and Elastic Net across Sets~3 and 4 (slope: LMM $+0.894/+0.861$, Elastic Net $+1.230/+0.993$; Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig2-attribution-lenses}, left). In contrast, $\mathit{topex}$ displays a pronounced split: LMM estimates a strong, stable positive effect ($+1.316/+1.323$), whereas Elastic Net yields weak, sign-flipping coefficients ($-0.175$ in Set~3 to $+0.063$ in Set~4) with high variance. We focus on $\mathit{topex}$ because it represents the clearest divergence among the six Set~4 variables displaying this cross-model disagreement (Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}). Two simpler explanations were ruled out first: multicollinearity does not explain the split (unstable predictors have \emph{lower} VIF, 2.1--3.4, than the stable rainfall metric's 3.91; full chart in Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}), and neither does climate-data timing (the static rainfall normal is the stable variable while the survey-matched $\mathit{tas\_mean}$ is unstable -- the opposite of what a timing explanation predicts -- and it does not touch $\mathit{soilgrids\_ph}$, a static soil trait, being unstable at all).
%TODO: add this static or changing through survey years in the data table.

\textbf{Spatial confounding} is the mechanism that survives: Elastic Net lacks random compartment intercepts and can conflate landscape gradients with unmeasured local stand factors. While unstable features all show high between-compartment variance ($\text{ICC} = 0.74\text{--}0.89$), stable rainfall exhibits an even higher ICC ($0.97$), showing that spatial clustering enables confounding but does not guarantee it in isolation.

%---
\textbf{The same mechanism -- whether a real local signal survives removing between-compartment differences -- also correctly sorts three further variables never checked when the mechanism was first proposed.} % AUDIT: this account was built and tested on the same data that produced the instability finding it explains -- a plausible, evidenced mechanism, not validated on an independent split. The extension below (ceh_twi, gwa_weibull_a_50m, local_relief_500m) is new evidence of generality, not just a re-statement of the same three cases -- see full table in Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}.
Because both models assume linear relationships, raw non-linearity alone cannot be the cause; the key difference is LMM's compartment random intercept. Mean-centring variables and targets within each compartment isolates this local signal directly, and checking Set4's full 19-variable list for EN/LMM sign disagreement surfaces three further unstable variables never checked when this mechanism was first proposed: $\mathit{ceh\_twi}$, $\mathit{gwa\_weibull\_a\_50m}$, and $\mathit{local\_relief\_500m}$. The same test sorts these the same way (summarised by the green/red ring colouring on Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig2-attribution-lenses}): $\mathit{topex}$ and $\mathit{gwa\_weibull\_a\_50m}$ retain a real local signal within compartments, while $\mathit{tas\_mean}$, $\mathit{soilgrids\_ph}$, $\mathit{ceh\_twi}$, and $\mathit{local\_relief\_500m}$ collapse toward zero -- their raw correlations are between-compartment artifacts. $\mathit{chelsa\_bio12\_precip\_mm}$, by contrast, keeps a clean local link, anchoring its stable coefficient despite high spatial variance. Full per-variable within-compartment correlations are in Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}.

Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig2-attribution-lenses} puts this coefficient comparison, the real-signal/artifact ring colouring just described, and XGBoost's own SHAP ranking side by side.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_results/q1/q1_final_fig2_attribution_three_lenses.png}
\caption{\textbf{Three lenses on Q1's attribution question (Set4, 4-survey).} Left: standardised EN (purple) and LMM (grey) coefficients, mean $\pm$ SD across 5 folds, hollow markers for Set3 and filled for Set4. LMM markers for the 6 genuinely disagreeing variables are ringed by mechanism verdict -- green where within-compartment correlation confirms a real local signal (topex), red where it collapses toward zero (tas\_mean, soilgrids\_ph, ceh\_twi, gwa\_weibull\_a\_50m, local\_relief\_500m). $\mathit{chelsa\_bio12\_precip\_mm}$ is left unringed: it is one of the two stable variables, not one of the six this mechanism explains. Right: XGBoost's own mean $|$SHAP$|$ ranking, same row order, for an independent third read on which variables the model actually leans on.}
\label{fig:q1-fig2-attribution-lenses}
\end{figure}

Apparent non-linearity in the pooled data is therefore a byproduct of spatial confounding. Variables with genuine local effects stay stable or resolve under random-intercept models, while those driven by between-compartment differences break down -- a pattern that held for three variables the mechanism was never built to explain, not just the three that motivated it (full 19-variable table in Appendix~\ref{app:nonlinearity-check}).
%---

\textbf{Both models leave significant spatial clustering in their residuals; XGBoost removes more of it overall, but the reduction is not a steady decline as environmental data is added.} All feature sets leave significant spatial autocorrelation in their residuals (distance-band Moran's $I$ at 1385--1739\,m, $p = 0.001$; Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig3-spatial-clustering}, Panel B). Comparing Set1 (stand-structure baseline) to Set4 (the full environmental set), Elastic Net drops residual clustering by 29\% (0.145 $\to$ 0.103) and XGBoost by 63\% (0.146 $\to$ 0.054). % THEORY, UNTESTED: XGBoost's own flexibility (automatic non-linear interactions) plausibly explains its larger overall reduction \cite{zou2005Regularization_C4_NN}, but the same flexibility could also just be fitting spatial noise -- not distinguished here.
But XGBoost's path there is not incremental: its single largest reduction happens already at Set2 (0.146 $\to$ 0.032, a 78\% drop), then partially reverses at Set3 (0.077) before falling again at Set4 (0.054) -- driven specifically by $\mathit{dist\_to\_road}$ and two climate variables absent from Set3, confirmed by ablation (removing them from Set4 pushes Moran's $I$ back to 0.084 for only a modest $R^2$ cost, 0.395 to 0.368). Elastic Net's own path is comparatively flat by contrast (0.103--0.110 across Set2--Set4). % AUDIT: corrected 2026-08-21 -- previous wording ("as environmental data is added") implied a smooth, incremental removal across Set1-Set4; the figure itself (Panel B's own subtitle) already flagged this as "not monotonic," but the text never mentioned it. Trimmed 2026-08-22 -- full ablation walkthrough moved out of main text; Figure~\ref{fig:q1-fig3-spatial-clustering} shows the non-monotonic shape directly.
Some clustering remains unmodelled in both cases, pointing to unmeasured environmental factors, resolution limits, or genuine spatially varying processes \cite{gaspard2019Residual_C5_EVAL}.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/fig_results/q1/q1_final_fig3_spatial_clustering.png}
\caption{\textbf{Spatial clustering by set, and what's left over (Set4, 4-survey).} \textbf{Panel A} (top): Set4's leftover Elastic Net residual, averaged to compartment level and mapped -- unexplained model error, not a validated local effect; the spatial pattern still visible here is what Q2 investigates directly. \textbf{Panel B} (bottom): residual Moran's $I$ by feature set, Elastic Net vs.\ XGBoost -- XGBoost's overall reduction is larger but not monotonic, dipping sharply at Set2 and partially rebounding at Set3.}
\label{fig:q1-fig3-spatial-clustering}
\end{figure}

Set~3 (terrain-only) is the weakest feature set. A category-level refit on Set~4 shows soil adds only a small gain ($+0.022$ $R^2$), while climate actively \emph{reduces} accuracy ($-0.056$ $R^2$) -- terrain and spatial-edge-effect variables drive most of Set~4's advantage instead (full ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:category-ablation}). This runs against the general expectation that forest productivity depends on mixed biophysical inputs \cite{bontemps2014Predictive_C2_BG}; here, climate data adds instability rather than predictive value.

Every environmental set's $R^2$ confidence interval clears the baseline (Set~1) with no overlap -- real evidence that environmental features help at all. But XGBoost's own intervals for Set~2 and Set~4 overlap ([0.355, 0.461] vs.\ [0.338, 0.438]), so which of those two sets is actually better cannot be said with confidence.

\subsection*{Conclusion}
Stand structure and management account for most of a plot's deviation from the baseline curve; among the abiotic variables examined in detail, slope and precipitation are consistently stable across methods, while six of Set4's 19 variables genuinely disagree between Elastic Net and the mixed-effects model. Instability depends on whether a genuine local signal survives between-compartment pooling: LMM recovers real local relationships for two of the six that Elastic Net obscures, while the other four are largely between-compartment artifacts (see Discussion for which is which). At the category level, soil adds a slight gain while climate harms performance. Significant spatial autocorrelation persists in both models' residuals (Moran's $I$ falls 29\% in EN vs.\ 63\% in XGBoost, though XGBoost's reduction is uneven across sets and driven disproportionately by $\mathit{dist\_to\_road}$ and climate variables rather than by predictive gain) -- global environmental features do not fully capture spatial structure, directly motivating the spatially varying model tested in Q2.
